title: Stripes on the seafloor
teaches: How magnetic reversals recorded in ocean-floor rock showed the sea floor spreading apart

blocks.text: In 1955 the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey ship *Pioneer* spent months sailing back and forth in closely spaced lines off the west coast of North America, mapping the depth of the sea floor for the Navy. Scientists from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography arranged to tow a magnetometer behind it, an instrument that measures the strength of the Earth's magnetic field. Because rocks containing iron minerals are slightly magnetic themselves, the field at the sea surface is a little stronger over some rocks and a little weaker over others.

When Ronald Mason and Arthur Raff drew up the survey off Washington, Oregon and northern California in 1961, the pattern was strange. Bands of stronger and weaker field ran roughly north to south, each a few kilometres to a few tens of kilometres wide and up to hundreds of kilometres long, like the stripes on a zebra. Some bands were offset sideways along east-west lines, as if the sea floor had been cut and shifted, and at the time no one had a convincing explanation for them.

blocks.caption: The sea floor off Washington and Oregon, shaded the same way as the land; the coast runs down the right third of the map. The red line follows the Juan de Fuca Ridge, which runs down the middle of the striped area. The map shows the shape of the sea floor rather than the magnetic stripes.

options.alt: A shaded relief map of the northeast Pacific off Washington and Oregon, showing the deep sea floor, a ridge running north-northeast about 400 kilometres offshore, the continental shelf, and Seattle and Portland inland.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Magnetic surveys off the Pacific Northwest revealed long, parallel stripes of stronger and weaker magnetism across the sea floor.

blocks.text: The rock of the ocean floor is **basalt** (lesson 4), which contains small grains of **magnetite**, a magnetic iron oxide. While lava is molten and very hot, thermal agitation keeps the magnetism of those grains scrambled. As the rock cools below about 580 °C, each grain's magnetism locks into alignment with the Earth's field at that moment and stays there, turning the cooled lava flow into a fossil compass that records which way the magnetic field pointed when the rock solidified.

blocks.caption: Pillow lava on the sea floor off Hawaii. Basalt erupted under water chills into rounded lobes like these.

blocks.text: Early in the twentieth century, geologists found something unexpected in such rocks. In 1906 the French physicist Bernard Brunhes found lavas in central France magnetised in the opposite direction to the present field, pointing south instead of north. In 1929 Motonori Matuyama found the same in lavas in Japan and Korea, and noticed that the reversed rocks were all older than the normal ones. The explanation, which took decades to win acceptance, is that the Earth's magnetic field itself flips, so that every so often the north and south magnetic poles trade places.

The field is generated by molten iron flowing in the Earth's outer core, where the motion is turbulent enough that the field occasionally breaks down and rebuilds the other way round. The intervals between flips are irregular, lasting anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of years. In the early 1960s two rival groups, Allan Cox, Richard Doell and Brent Dalrymple in California, and Ian McDougall and Don Tarling in Australia, dated lava flows from around the world using the radioactive decay of potassium to argon and recorded each flow's magnetic direction. Their work built a timescale of reversals: the last flip was about 780,000 years ago, and before that the field had been mostly reversed for nearly two million years, interrupted by a few shorter normal spells.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: As basalt cools below about 580 °C, magnetite grains lock in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.
The magnetic field reverses at irregular intervals; the most recent reversal occurred about 780,000 years ago.
Radiometric dating of magnetised lava flows on land establishes a timeline of past reversals.

blocks.text: While the reversal timescale was being assembled, the American geologist Harry Hess proposed in a paper circulated in 1960 and published in 1962 what Robert Dietz in 1961 named **seafloor spreading**. Hess suggested that the long ridges in the middle of the oceans are places where hot mantle rock rises, partly melts, and erupts to form new basalt crust. That crust then moves away on both sides of the ridge, carried along by the slow circulation of the mantle beneath, widening the ocean basin. Because the Earth is not expanding, old ocean floor must eventually sink back into the mantle somewhere else.

blocks.caption: The Almannagjá rift at Þingvellir, Iceland, where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above the sea and the ground is being pulled apart.

blocks.text: In 1963 Fred Vine, a graduate student at Cambridge, and his supervisor Drummond Matthews combined seafloor spreading with magnetic reversals, an idea that the Canadian geophysicist Lawrence Morley had reached independently a few months earlier only to have two journals reject his paper. If new crust forms at a ridge and spreads outward while the Earth's magnetic field periodically flips, each strip of cooling basalt will record the direction of the field at the time it formed. The sea floor should therefore be striped in bands of normal and reversed magnetisation running parallel to the ridge, forming mirror images on the two sides like a twin tape recording wound outward from the centre. Rock magnetised in the same direction as today's field adds slightly to the magnetic strength a ship measures at the surface, whereas rock magnetised the opposite way subtracts from it, so a magnetometer towed across the ridge records a rising and falling curve.

blocks.caption: A spreading ridge. New crust takes on the direction of the field (dark: normal, as today; pale: reversed) and moves away on both sides. Top: the magnetic field a ship would measure; the dotted line is a survey to match.
blocks.task: Find the spreading rate that matches the survey

blocks.text: Spreading rates are quoted either for one side of a ridge (the half-rate, used in the diagram above) or for both sides combined (the full rate). The Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis can be tested directly against the map: the magnetic stripes across a ridge should be symmetrical about the crest, and the width of each stripe should equal the duration of that magnetic interval multiplied by the spreading rate. In 1965 and 1966 both predictions held up. Vine and the Canadian geologist J. Tuzo Wilson matched the stripes across the Juan de Fuca Ridge, right in the middle of Mason and Raff's survey, to the land-based reversal timescale. Soon after, Walter Pitman at Lamont Geological Observatory in New York produced a magnetic profile across the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge from the research ship *Eltanin* that was so symmetrical across the ridge axis that it won over many of the remaining sceptics on sight. The profile even preserved a brief normal interval around a million years ago, the Jaramillo, which had just been identified in lavas in New Mexico.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: New basalt crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads away on both sides, recording magnetic reversals as parallel stripes.
The stripes on opposite sides of a ridge are mirror images whose widths match the land-based reversal timescale.
Dividing a stripe's width by the duration of its magnetic interval gives the spreading rate, typically a few centimetres a year on each side.

parts.title: The age of the ocean floor

blocks.text: The stripes gave geologists a way to read the age of the ocean floor from a ship without ever touching the rock. Once the reversal timescale was extended further into the past, each numbered magnetic stripe in the world's oceans could be assigned a date, allowing maps of the age of the entire oceanic crust to be drawn. Those maps show young rock along the ridge crests and progressively older rock toward the continental margins, just as seafloor spreading requires.

In 1968 the scientific drilling ship *Glomar Challenger* tested these ages directly during an expedition across the South Atlantic. Sailing between Africa and South America, it drilled down through the soft seafloor mud at a series of sites at increasing distances from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge until the drill bit hit the underlying basalt, and dated the oldest sediment resting directly on the volcanic rock using the fossil shells of microscopic plankton. The age of that bottom layer of sediment increased steadily with distance from the ridge, matching the ages predicted from the magnetic stripes above.

blocks.caption: The drilling ship Glomar Challenger, with its tall derrick amidships.
Full spreading rates, counting both sides of the ridge, compared with familiar speeds.

blocks.text: Aside from a few older remnants trapped in the Mediterranean, the oldest ocean floor in the main ocean basins is only about 180 million years old, in the western Pacific and along the margins of the North Atlantic. Continents preserve rocks up to four billion years old, whereas the ocean basins are geologically young throughout, because oceanic crust is continually destroyed as well as created. Meanwhile the Atlantic continues to widen by a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow, carrying the Americas away from Europe and Africa. That answered the mechanical objection that had dogged Alfred Wegener's continental drift: continents move as passengers embedded in larger spreading plates rather than ploughing through solid ocean floor. Where the old sea floor goes when its journey ends is the subject of the next lesson.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Deep-sea drilling in 1968 confirmed that the ocean floor gets steadily older with distance from mid-ocean ridges.
Oceanic crust in the major basins is no more than about 180 million years old, showing that old sea floor is recycled back into the mantle.
Continents move across the globe as part of rigid plates that spread apart at ridges.

blocks.caption: Five questions on seafloor spreading
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: How does a basalt lava flow record the direction of the Earth's magnetic field?
choices: Magnetite grains lock in the field's direction as the lava cools below about 580 °C
The lava flows downhill in the direction of magnetic north
Iron-rich minerals settle toward the north side of the molten flow
items.why: Above about 580 °C thermal motion keeps the magnetism of magnetite grains scrambled; on cooling below that temperature, their magnetic alignment freezes in line with the ambient field.

items.ask: Why are the magnetic stripes on one side of a mid-ocean ridge a mirror image of the stripes on the other side?
choices: Crust formed along the ridge axis splits and is carried away equally in both directions
The Earth's magnetic field is stronger on one side of the ridge than the other
Ocean currents flowing along the ridge align the sediment in symmetrical bands
items.why: Each strip of new crust cools and locks in the current magnetic field along the ridge crest before splitting as newer magma intrudes, sending matching halves to either side.

items.ask: A band of ocean crust that took 1.8 million years to form is 54 km wide on one side of a ridge. What was the half-spreading rate on that side?
items.why: 54 km divided by 1.8 million years is 30 km per million years, which equals 30 mm (3 cm) a year.

items.ask: What did the Glomar Challenger find when it drilled down to the basalt at increasing distances from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
choices: The lowest layer of sediment resting on the basalt got steadily older away from the ridge
The sediment layer had the same age at every site across the ocean
The basalt was oldest at the ridge crest and youngest near the continents
items.why: Plankton shells begin settling onto new basalt as soon as it cools at the ridge, so the age of the sediment directly touching the basalt records when that patch of crust formed.

items.ask: Why is almost all ocean floor less than 180 million years old, whereas continents contain rocks up to four billion years old?
choices: Old ocean floor sinks back into the mantle elsewhere as fast as new crust forms at ridges
The ocean basins only filled with water about 180 million years ago
Older ocean floor has been buried beneath continental sediment by erosion
items.why: Because the Earth's surface area is constant, the continuous creation of oceanic crust at spreading ridges requires an equal rate of destruction where old crust descends into the mantle.

summary: **Cooling lava records the magnetic field.** Basalt locks in the field’s direction as it cools.
**The field reverses.** North and south swap at irregular intervals, many times over Earth’s history.
**New ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges.** It spreads away on both sides, carrying the record with it.
**Reversals make matching stripes.** The sea floor shows symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of a ridge.
**Stripe widths give spreading rates.** Matched to the reversal timescale, they show a few centimetres a year.
**Ocean floor is young.** Nowhere older than about 180 million years in the main basins, so old floor must be destroyed elsewhere.
